title: fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule allocates final_state for one sequence but writes it for the whole batch, resulting in out-of-bounds writes
body: `fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_fwd` allocates the non-inplace final state with `T` rows, but the kernel stores the state after every token at row `bos + i_t`, with `bos = i_n * T`. For a fixed-length batch (`cu_seqlens=None`) with `B > 1`, sequences `n >= 1` write rows `n*T ... n*T+T-1`, which are past the end of the `T`-row buffer.
label: bug

title: KV offload back-pressure ignores failed secondary-tier stores, so a full filesystem tier keeps receiving every cascade
body: `TieringOffloadingManager` only reports **successful** primary→secondary store completions to the tier's `BackpressureDetector` (added in #50045): https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/a9fe30e9f6f73a982eab0730476df165484ad4d4/vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/manager.py#L545-L546 `EMABackpressureDetector` is driven only by store latency. A tier that rejects writes does not get slow; it fails fast. A typical case is a shared filesystem tier that has filled up (`ENOSPC`) or hit a directory quota (`EDQUOT`). For example, an external evictor such as the llm-d PVC evictor has a soft threshold, and the volume can reach 100% before it frees space (llm-d/llm-d-kv-cache#218). In that state: 1. No latency samples arrive, so the EMA never crosses the high water mark. 2. If the detector already reached the healthy fast-path (`_HEALTHY_THRESHOLD` fast completions), `should_store()` returns `True` without consulting the policy. `_healthy_streak` is only reset by a slow *successful* completion, so the tier stays "healthy" for as long as every store fails. 3. If the tier fails from its very first store, warmup never completes. Pressure can never be signalled at all. As a result, every cascade keeps going to the failing tier. Each store job pins the primary chunks, and for the `fs` tier it also runs `exists` + `makedirs` + `open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL)` and then the temp-file cleanup against a filesystem that is already in trouble. Each job also logs `Job ... block I/O failed: [Errno 28] No space left on device` at ERROR level. Back-pressure, which is meant to protect a struggling tier, is effectively disabled exactly when the tier is unwritable. The job-failure metrics in `TieringMetricsTracker` do count these failures, so operators can see them. Nothing acts on them, though. **Where it shows up in practice** (the `fs` tier on a filesystem that runs out of space, with back-pressure enabled): Once the filesystem is full, every cascade is still submitted to the tier and fails with `Errno 28`. title: `lightning_attention` prefill applies one decay step too few to the stored state (tokens after position 256 wrong, and every token when continuing from a non-zero `kv_history`)
body: **Summary.** `lightning_attention` (`vllm/model_executor/layers/lightning_attn.py`) computes the linear-attention recurrence `kv_t = exp(-s)·kv_{t-1} + k_tᵀv_t`, `o_t = q_t·kv_t` in 256-token blocks. In `_fwd_none_diag_kernel`, the stored-state contribution to query offset `c` in a block is scaled by `q_decay = exp(-s * c)`. But the stored state is the state at the token *before* the block (the last token of the previous block, or the incoming `kv_history` for the first block), which is `c + 1` steps back. So the history term is off by a factor of `exp(s)`. - Without `kv_history`: every token from position 256 on is wrong. - With a non-zero `kv_history`: every token of the first block is wrong too, so a short prefill chunk continuing from a stored state is wrong from its very first token. **Who hits this.** It's the prefill path of `MiniMaxText01LinearKernel.jit_linear_forward_prefix`, used in 0.31.0 by `BailingMoeV2_5ForCausalLM` (and the MiniMax-Text-01/M1 linear-attention layers it was written for), with fp32 q/k/v as the model passes them. That function passes the request's stored state as `kv_history` (`minimax_linear_attn.py:141-143`), so two kinds of call are affected: any prompt or chunk longer than 256 tokens, and any chunk starting from a non-zero stored state (e.g. later chunks of a chunked prefill). For reference, the decode kernel (`linear_decode_forward_triton`) and the HF transformers MiniMax implementation (`query_decay = exp(-slope * (arange(block_size) + 1))`) both use the `c + 1` convention. `tests/kernels/attention/test_lightning_attn.py` does pass a `kv_history`, so its own 16-token input hits the second case, but it still passes because the inputs are scaled by 0.01 and the tolerance is `atol=rtol=0.15`. This isn't a convention difference: within the same call, tokens 0..255 (the diagonal-block kernel) match the standard recurrence to fp32 level, while tokens from 256 on (the stored-state path) don't, so the kernel is inconsistent with itself.
label: bug

title: tiering async lookup serves stale absent verdicts across instances sharing a secondary tier
body: When the secondary tier says a key is absent, AsyncLookupManager caches that and keeps it until no request references the key. A new request for the same key in that window gets the cached absent and never probes. That works fine for a private tier but not a shared one (fs root_dir, obj). Another instance can write the block right after the probe. With steady traffic on a common prefix some request always holds the key, so this instance keeps missing blocks that are already on disk. Repro on main, cpu only. The set stands in for the shared tier, and adding the key is another instance writing the block: observed: expected: r2 never reaches the backend, and same with the real fs tier: two processes, each with its own `FileSystemTierManager` on one shared `root_dir`. A stores 4 chunks while B's r1 is alive. Proposed fix: a new request gets a fresh probe instead of inheriting a resolved absent verdict. Present verdicts and in-flight probes stay shared, so the probe reuse from #55823 is kept. A ttl on absent verdicts is the alternative.
label: bug

title: `--shutdown-timeout` never drains in-flight requests when `--api-server-count > 1`: the launcher stops the API servers before the engines, so every in-flight request fails with EngineDeadError and the engines then drain for nobody
body: `--shutdown-timeout N` is documented as "Shutdown will be delayed for up to this amount of time to allow already-running requests to complete" (`vllm/config/vllm.py`). With a single API server that is what happens: on SIGTERM the API server keeps streaming while `MPClient.shutdown` waits for the engine, the engine enters `mode=drain`, finishes the admitted requests and rejects new ones. With `--api-server-count > 1` (which is also the default whenever `--data-parallel-size > 1`), the same flag has no effect on in-flight requests. They all fail immediately with HTTP 500 / `EngineDeadError`, and the engines then spend up to N seconds "draining" requests whose clients already received errors. `run_multi_api_server` (`vllm/entrypoints/cli/serve.py`) tears down in this order: Each API server worker handles SIGTERM in `vllm/entrypoints/launchers/launcher.py::handle_shutdown` by calling `engine_client.shutdown(timeout=N)`. In multi-server mode the engines are owned by the launcher, so the worker's `MPClient.resources.engine_manager` is `None`: `MPClient.shutdown` (`vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py`) has nothing to wait for and immediately runs `self.resources()`, which marks the engine dead, closes the ZMQ sockets and cancels the output queue task. The cancelled task enqueues `EngineDeadError`, `AsyncLLM.output_handler` propagates it to every waiting `generate()` call, and all in-flight requests return 500. Only then does step 2 send SIGTERM to the engines, which log `[shutdown] EngineCore: draining in-flight requests ...` and keep computing outputs on PUSH sockets that no longer have a peer, until the requests finish or the N seconds run out. In single-server mode the order is reversed by construction: `MPClient.shutdown` first waits for `engine_manager.shutdown(timeout=N)` (the engine drains while the API server's event loop keeps relaying outputs) and only then closes its sockets. body: Reproduced on main at 5555a2d8f (editable install with the precompiled kernels), NVIDIA driver 617.42, which `collect_env` does not pick up from the WSL `nvidia-smi`. With `truncation_side` unset, the tokenizer truncates the prompt itself and keeps them. The side doesn't have to differ from the tokenizer's default; spelling out the default is enough. title: Greedy (temperature=0) decoding is not reproducible across repeated calls on the same engine for LiquidAI/LFM2-8B-A1B (hybrid mamba)
body: On `LiquidAI/LFM2-8B-A1B` (hybrid conv + SSM + full-attention), **greedy decoding is not reproducible**: with the same engine instance, same seed and same prompts, `temperature=0` produces different token sequences across repeated `generate()` calls. The batch is identical across rounds; the only difference is time (and therefore kernel/scheduling order). The divergence signature is consistent across every mismatching prompt: **a long identical prefix, a single differing token, then re-alignment** — the classic signature of a nondeterministic reduction order (atomicAdd / split-K accumulation) perturbing logits just enough to flip an argmax. title: Request observer hook for the Rust frontend
body: We run vLLM behind an API gateway and collect per-tenant usage records (prompt / cached / generated tokens) in an L7 proxy in front of it today. With the Rust frontend we would rather do this in process, as an out-of-tree module (a small crate that plugs into the frontend and writes usage records to our own store): the frontend knows the exact token counts without parsing responses, including for streams the client aborts before the final usage chunk is sent, which a proxy never sees. We don't want to patch vLLM for this, so upstream would only need a narrow, generic hook. In the Python frontend this is possible out of tree: a stat logger plugin (`vllm.stat_logger_plugins`) receives per-request `FinishedRequestStats`, and `--middleware` can map the tenant by request id. title: Improve engine RPC failure handling and shutdown
body: When one worker returns an RPC error, other workers may still have replies pending. Returning immediately can leave those replies for the next call, while waiting without a deadline can block indefinitely. If reply collection cannot finish, the executor must stop accepting work, callers must receive the failure, and workers must be cleaned up. This proposal connects reply collection, failure propagation, and cleanup around two outcomes: The timeout branch is deliberately conservative: a reply missing at the reply collection deadline makes the executor unusable, even if the worker is only delayed. This extends terminal-failure handling to RPC response timeouts, using the existing executor-failure callback and Core/process-manager shutdown path. Both outcomes depend on the following four changes. Worker RPC replies are matched to calls by queue order. If RPC A returns after reading one worker's error, RPC B can consume an unread reply from A: Record the first error encountered in reply-queue order, then finish consuming **one reply from each worker selected for RPC A**, counting both successful and failed replies. Return the recorded error after collection completes, leaving replies for later RPCs untouched. RPC A still fails, but a subsequent operation can read its own replies. Collecting those remaining replies requires a limit on waiting. Another worker may be a straggler, still alive but slow to reply, or may never respond. After the first worker error, apply one reply collection deadline. Share the remaining time across all selected workers and receive stages, preserving any earlier caller deadline. If the reply collection deadline expires, fail the executor and block both queued and new RPCs from reusing the response queues. Blocking further RPCs does not release callers already waiting for results. Fail queued worker RPC futures when the executor becomes unusable. title: Support sharing SimpleCPUOffload prefix caches across local DP replicas
body: `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector` (#37160) keeps a private CPU prefix cache per DP replica. Unlike the native `OffloadingConnector`, the Simple connector is agnostic to KV organization and adapts to day-0 models without per-model integration, which makes it a natural fit for throughput-oriented DP-heavy deployments (e.g. 8×H100 with DP8/TP1/EP). In such deployments each replica's CPU KV pool is small, and identical prefixes are recomputed whenever a request is routed to a different local replica, even though a completed CPU copy exists on the same host. Sharing the local CPU pool would let these deployments draw on a larger combined KV pool instead of many small private ones. Measured on a diagnostic DP4/TP1/EP topology (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, two hosts, two logical workers sharing each physical GB10 GPU — timings are diagnostic, not production throughput numbers). Routing a repeated ~6K-token prefix to a peer replica costs **14.41 s TTFT (full recompute)**; with shared offload it costs **5.22 s (91.7% of prompt tokens restored via external KV transfer)** — a 63.8% reduction. body: `vllm bench serve` records the model in its `--output-json` payload: `vllm bench latency` and `vllm bench throughput` do not. Their payloads are: So a latency or throughput result file does not say which model produced the numbers. Any consumer that archives, compares, or ingests these files has to recover the model out-of-band — from the output filename, or from the shell command that produced it. Both are lossy: filenames are chosen by the caller, and the command is not stored next to the result. This bites in CI/benchmark-tracking setups, where result files are collected from many runs and loaded into a database. title: Add a CPU-only Wide Expert Parallelism well-lit path
body: Add functional Expert Parallelism (EP), including DP-attention + EP-MoE deployments, to the vLLM CPU backend. The CPU backend currently appears to partially wire up Expert Parallelism, but the default CPU all-to-all path cannot complete because the variable-size collectives required by `AgRsAll2AllManager` are not implemented by `CpuCommunicator`. The goal is to support CPU-only MoE deployments across multiple ranks/nodes, including use cases such as llm-d Wide Expert Parallelism on x86_64 servers. This does **not** require porting DeepEP to CPU. A functional CPU communication backend using `torch.distributed`, Gloo, oneCCL, or another appropriate CPU transport would be sufficient as an initial implementation. `CpuCommunicator` already detects EP/all-to-all usage and selects the generic `AgRsAll2AllManager`: GPU-specific all-to-all backends are also explicitly rejected/fallen back to `allgather_reducescatter` on CPU. However, `AgRsAll2AllManager` requires variable-size collectives: for dispatch, and: for combine. `CpuCommunicator` currently implements regular `all_gather()`, but does not override `all_gatherv()` or `reduce_scatterv()`. The implementations inherited from `DeviceCommunicatorBase` raise `NotImplementedError`. As a result, the CPU backend appears to have the EP/AgRs plumbing in place, but no functional implementation of the communication primitives required for DP+EP execution. `--enable-expert-parallel` should work with the CPU backend using the `allgather_reducescatter` backend, initially without requiring EPLB. body: Tracking issue for the `GenerateLogProbs` shape redesign. @sagearc raised it on #42729 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4547904742). `/inference/v1/generate` is a vLLM defined token in / token out API (#24261) but its output logprobs use an OpenAI shape. `GenerateResponseChoice.logprobs` and `GenerateResponseStreamChoice.logprobs` are `ChatCompletionLogProbs` where `token` is a string. The generate server has no tokenizer, so it writes every token as a `"token_id:N"` placeholder and derender parses the placeholders back out. This causes a few problems: - **The OpenAI shape leaks into a vLLM protocol.** Converting to OpenAI's string tokens belongs in derender (or the coupled chat / completions path), not on the generate server. - **The format is an untyped string contract.** On the encoding side it's `_create_tokens_logprobs` in Python and `format_token_id` in the Rust frontend's `routes/inference/generate.rs`. title: Parser cache for streaming chat derender and stable tool call IDs on retried calls
body: Tracking issue for work deferred from the streaming derender RFC #47161 and PR #50550: server side parser state for streaming chat derender, and keeping tool call IDs stable when a chunk is retried. With a reasoning or tool parser configured, streaming chat derender keeps nothing on the server. Each chunk builds a fresh parser, replays the history the client echoes back in `stream_state` (`output_token_ids`, split by `output_chunk_lens`) through `parse_delta`, then feeds the new chunk (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat_stream_parsed`). Any replica can serve any chunk and the client carried state is the only source of truth. The price is replay. It's O(n²) `parse_delta` calls over a generation and O(n³) character work for parsers that re-scan accumulated text (Hermes tool call JSON, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning). The "Streaming cost" section of `derenderer.md` documents this. @shimib measured it on 1×A100-40G with Qwen3-8B and the hermes + qwen3 parsers (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033): ~9× the in-process CPU at matched load, +15% E2E p50 on multi-thousand-token reasoning outputs and a saturated tier under concurrent parsed streams with the default `renderer_num_workers=1`. Latency sensitive P/D goes to #56851 where the parser lives with the request on the decode pool and there's no replay. This issue covers the consumers that keep using streaming derender: RL, batch and gateways that own postprocessing. title: Production evidence for restoring concurrent partial prefill limits (max_num_partial_prefills / max_concurrent_prefills) in V1 scheduler
body: We operate a production vLLM deployment (GLM-based MoE model, TP=4, 4x NVIDIA B200, V1 engine) serving a workload dominated by very long prompts (RAG/long-context, median ~100k-180k prompt tokens per request, generation typically <1k tokens). Under this workload we consistently observe severe TTFT tail latency caused by head-of-line blocking in prefill scheduling, and we believe this is a strong real-world case for reviving #49075 / #55256. With `--enable-chunked-prefill` and `--max-num-batched-tokens` set to a reasonably high value (tested 8192 and 16384), a single long-prompt request still needs many scheduler iterations to complete its prefill (prompt_tokens / max_num_batched_tokens ≈ 7-12 iterations for our 100k-180k token prompts). Because the V1 scheduler currently has **no cap on concurrent partial prefills**, any request queued behind one of these long prefills must wait for it to fully finish before its own prefill can start — there is no way to interleave multiple partial prefills to give newer/shorter requests a fair share of the per-step token budget. We attempted to mitigate this with `--max-num-partial-prefills 4` (docs suggest this exists as a `SchedulerConfig` field), which immediately fails: vllm: error: unrecognized arguments: --max-num-partial-prefills 4 Digging into this, we found the flag was intentionally removed from `vllm/config/scheduler.py` in #49244 (V0 cleanup, July 2026) as "dead config" because it had no V1 consumer, and issue #39737 confirms the same failure mode on an earlier vLLM version (`NotImplementedError: Concurrent Partial Prefill is not supported`) with no maintainer response since April 2026. #49075 attempts to restore and properly enforce these fields in the V1 scheduler but is currently open, unrebased, has an unresolved CodeRabbit finding on the WAITING-loop admission check, and has never had CI run. #55256 proposed a simpler, threshold-independent `max_concurrent_prefills` knob with a supporting benchmark, but was closed

title: BLOCK_SIZE_K=128 decode default causes large slowdown on Volta/V100
body: I am filing this as a performance discussion rather than a bug report because V100 / `sm_70` is not a primary target for current vLLM wheels. The useful upstream part is a measured fused-MoE default/config finding that affects the V100-relevant vLLM line. The focus is vLLM 0.19, because that is the last broadly practical vLLM line for Tesla V100 users. I also verified the same fused-MoE default shape in my 0.21 source-build path, but I am not asking vLLM to restore V100 wheel support here. Summary: 1. **Finding** - On Tesla V100 / Volta (`sm_70`), the fused-MoE decode/small-M path using `BLOCK_SIZE_K=128` is much slower than expected. - The practical symptom is that FP16/BF16 sparse MoE decode can become slower than dense models of similar class. - This is not the hardware limit itself; it is a bad fallback/default for Volta. 2. **Measured fix** - For small-M decode on Volta, changing the MoE tile to `BLOCK_SIZE_K=64` removes the pathology. - In my A/B tests, output remained bit-identical. - This is a speed/config fix, not an approximation. 3. **Suggested upstream path** - If vLLM is willing to accept V100 config data, I can provide tuned config JSONs for Tesla V100. - I am not proposing an sm_70 support-policy change. - If heuristic code for sm_70 is not in scope, the data/config contribution may still be useful. The main question for maintainers: Would vLLM accept V100 fused-MoE config JSONs / performance data for the 0.19-era Volta path, or is this better kept as external documentation only? title: Tracking GLM-5.1-FP8 Triton MoE Decode Optimizations on H20
body: This issue tracks follow-up Triton fused MoE optimizations for GLM-5.1-FP8 on NVIDIA H20 after PR [#46189](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46189). PR #46189 adds a Hopper `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE` backend and already improves the attention side substantially over `origin/main`, especially for BS1 and BS8 decode-heavy shapes. **After that attention improvement, local profiling still shows meaningful decode time inside the Triton fused MoE payload, so the remaining work here is focused on MoE kernel/config/runtime improvements rather than attention.** The planned work is intentionally split into small PRs. The first PR should add role-specific W13/W2 Triton MoE config lookup because it is the smallest correctness-preserving change. Later PRs can evaluate the more invasive W2/down TMA path and SM90 `swap_ab` FP8 dot path separately. Environment used for the local prototype: GLM-5.1-FP8, NVIDIA H20, tensor parallel size 8, `vllm bench serve`, BS in `{1, 8, 64}`, ISL in `{512, 4096}`, OSL in `{512, 4096}`, primary metric mean TPOT ms. Motivation: The Triton fused MoE path currently selects one tuned config for both W13/gate-up projection and W2/down projection. These two invocations have different effective dimensions and resource tradeoffs, so one shared config can become a compromise. For GLM-5.1-FP8/H20 TP8 decode, W13 benefits from smaller `BLOCK_SIZE_N`, while W2 benefits from shallower staging. Plan: Add a generic role-aware config lookup, for example `moe_op=w13` and `moe_op=w2`, while preserving fallback to existing shared config files when role-specific configs are absent. The first tuned entries can include the locally validated GLM-5.1-FP8/H20 choices, such as W13 `BLOCK_SIZE_N=64` and W2 `num_stages=2`, if maintainers agree that hardware/model-specific config data should be included with the mechanism. This should not change math semantics, routing, tensor values, or top-k behavior. Add focused tests for lookup priority and fallback behavior. Motivati

Based on brief investigation, this seems to impact only multimodal models because thread safe tokenizer pool introduced in mentioned PR is applied in HFRenderer.__init__.py. It seems that the root cause is that deep copy of tokenizer is made every time tokenizer pool (where are already created tokenizer copies) is drained, so for benchmarks where many concurrent requests are sent this issue happens. title: Triton unified attention: sliding-window / chunked KV-tile loop iterates an extra tile when the window start is not tile-aligned
body: In `triton_unified_attention.py`, the sliding-window / chunked-attention KV-tile loop starts at a floor-rounded tile boundary (`first_allowed_key // TILE_SIZE`) rather than at the window's first allowed key. The leading slots before `first_allowed_key` in that first tile are masked out by `seq_mask`, but they still consume part of the tile, so a window of `W` keys can span one more `TILE_SIZE` tile than the minimal `ceil(W / TILE_SIZE)`. `compute_tile_loop_bounds` (`triton_attention_helpers.py`): paired with the main loop: A window of `W = last_allowed_key - first_allowed_key + 1` keys starting at residue `r = first_allowed_key % TILE_SIZE` spans `ceil((r + W) / TILE_SIZE)` tiles with the floor-rounded start, versus the minimal `ceil(W / TILE_SIZE)` if iteration begins at `first_allowed_key` - up to one extra tile iteration (KV load + MMA + softmax merge). No tile is fully masked; the first tile is partially masked at its front, and that misalignment is what pushes the window's tail into the extra tile. Example (`TILE_SIZE = 32`, window `[31, 46]`, `W = 16`, `r = 31`): floor-rounded start iterates tiles `{0, 1}` (the window's keys split 1 + 15); a window-aligned start iterates 1. Have `compute_tile_loop_bounds` return a base offset `tile_base` and iterate `seq_offset = tile_base + j * TILE_SIZE + offs_t`, beginning exactly at `first_allowed_key`. The window then occupies the minimal `ceil(W / TILE_SIZE)` tiles. - Non-SWA paths and the 3D-segmented SWA path are unchanged (`tile_base = 0`; the 3D path reasons in absolute tile indices). - The tensor-descriptor (`USE_TD`) path is also unchanged (`tile_base = 0`): its KV load fetches a whole tile from one block and relies on `BLOCK_SIZE % TILE_SIZE == 0`, which an arbitrary base would break. - Only the 2D pointer sliding-window / chunked path shifts its base; its per-slot `physical_block_idx = seq_offset // BLOCK_SIZE` load already handles a tile straddling two blocks. title: FlashInfer AR+RMSNorm fusion cap is ~2x too high on multimem NVLink Hopper (TP8): it displaces the faster multimem all-reduce in the 256KB-512KB band
body: On a multimem/NVSwitch sm90 node at TP8 (default settings), `AllReduceFusionPass` fuses `all_reduce + residual + RMSNorm` into flashinfer's one-shot trtllm AR whenever the message is below `FI_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_MAX_SIZE_MB[90][8] = 0.5 MB`. But above **256 KB** the *unfused* all-reduce uses vLLM's fast `multimem_all_reduce` (NVLink multicast), which is faster than flashinfer's one-shot AR. So in the **256 KB–512 KB** band the pass trades the fast `multimem` AR for a slower fused AR — a net regression: - **−1.9 to −4.3 µs/op** (microbench, CUDA-graph timed) - **−3.4 % / −7.4 % decode throughput at batch 96 / 128** (Qwen3-30B-A3B, TP8) Fix: cap the fusion at the size where the fast unfused AR takes over (256 KB here), gated on multimem availability. 8×H200 (sm_90), NVLink/NVSwitch, TP8, bf16. vLLM `0.1.dev1916`, flashinfer `0.6.11.post2`. Defaults `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM=1`, `VLLM_USE_NCCL_SYMM_MEM=0`, `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0`. `cuda_communicator.all_reduce` sends the unfused AR to vLLM's custom one-shot kernel below `CUSTOM_ALL_REDUCE_MAX_SIZES["9.0"][8] = 262144 B` and to `multimem_all_reduce` at/above it (the NCCL-symm-mem and flashinfer-regular-AR branches are off by default). `AllReduceFusionPass` emits flashinfer's one-shot trtllm AR+RMSNorm for any message below `FI_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_MAX_SIZE_MB[90][8] = 0.5 MB`. So in 256 KB–512 KB the pass replaces the fast `multimem` AR with the slower flashinfer one-shot; the ~2 µs RMSNorm saving doesn't offset flashinfer being ~2× slower than `multimem` there. **1. title: Massive increase (~10x) in KV Cache capacity for Gemma 4 in v0.21.0
body: _No response_ _No response_ **Obersvation** While testing Gemma 4 (specifically using [cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit](https://huggingface.co/cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-4bit)) on an A100 80GB, I observed a massive increase in available KV cache capacity between vLLM v0.20.0 and v0.21.0. **Comparison Data** Using the same args and `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9`: | vLLM Version | GPU KV Cache Size | Memory Cost per Token | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **v0.20.0** | ~55k tokens | High | | **v0.21.0** | ~525k tokens | Low (~9.5x reduction) | Total available KV cache memory remained constant (~50 GB), indicating the efficiency gain is per token. **Technical Analysis** Gemma 4 utilizes several advanced memory-saving features: 1. **Alternating Attention:** Mix of local sliding-window layers (1024 tokens) and global full-context layers. 2. **Shared KV Cache:** The last $N$ layers reuse KV states from earlier layers. 3. **Dual RoPE:** Standard RoPE for sliding layers and pruned RoPE for global layers. (Source: [Hugging Face Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/gemma4)) It appears that in v0.20.0, the memory profiler may have been treating all layers as global and non-shared, leading to massive over-allocation. In v0.21.0, vLLM seems to correctly recognize the sliding-window budget and shared KV states, unlocking the actual capacity of the architecture. **Request** This is a massive win for performance and deployment density. I suggest documenting this improvement in the release notes or the model support page so users know to upgrade for Gemma 4. **Suggested wording** > Users upgrading from vLLM v0.20.0 to v0.21.0 will notice a significant increase in available KV cache capacity for Gemma 4 (roughly 9.5x). This is due to optimized support for Gemma 4's unique architecture, including alternating sliding-window attention and shared KV states, which drastically reduces the memory cost per token.

title: Triton fusion for Qwen2/3-MoE shared-expert gate (Qwen2MoeMLP/Qwen3MoeMLP)
body: In `vllm/model_executor/models/qwen2_moe.py:119-120` (also reused by `qwen3_next.py` via re-export of `Qwen2MoeMLP`) and the byte-identical duplicate in `qwen3_moe.py:131-132`, the shared-expert gate runs as: For Qwen3-Next configs (`shared_expert_gate = ReplicatedLinear(H, 1)` → `weight.shape == [1, H]`), this expands at runtime into three back-to-back memory-bound GPU kernels (skinny `[N,H]×[H,1]` GEMM → sigmoid on `[N,1]` → broadcast multiply `[N,1]·[N,H]`) plus two HBM-resident intermediates. A single Triton kernel that does one row at a time — load `x_row`, load `weight`, compute `sigmoid(dot)`, load `out_row`, store `out_row * gate` — collapses them into one pass and removes both intermediates. I have a working patch (Triton kernel + Python wrapper with a shape-guard fallback + parametrized correctness test) and a full A/B sweep on MI355x — numbers in the "Misc" section. This is complementary to #39280 (AITER FSE) rather than overlapping. FSE (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS`, default `False`) bypasses the call site at the MoE-block level when the user is on ROCm + AITER **and** has explicitly opted in. title: Inconsistent hash notation in Prefix Caching "Time 5" diagram
body: In the [Automatic Prefix Caching documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/#example), there is an inconsistency in how block hashes are labeled in the example diagrams, specifically transitioning from Time 4 to Time 5. The core concept of prefix caching is that a block's hash is built using the parent hash (prefix) + the block tokens. In the Time 4 diagram, the Hash values inside the Block Pool correctly use the prefix notation (e.g., Block 0 is A-D, Block 1 is A-H, Block 3 is A-P). This perfectly matches the Cache Blocks (dict) on the left side. In the Time 5 diagram ("Request 1 is finished and free"), the Hash values inside the Block Pool suddenly switch to showing the local block tokens instead of the prefix hash (e.g., Block 0 becomes ABCD, Block 1 becomes EFGH, Block 2 becomes IJKL). The Time 5 diagram should be updated so that the Block Pool boxes display the correct prefix hashes (A-D, A-H, A-L, A-P, A-J,kl, etc) to remain consistent with Time 4. I am a new contributor and would love to help fix this! I can edit the source diagram to correct the labels and open a Pull Request. Please let me know if I should go ahead and submit the PR.

title: Speculative decoding --speculative-config option lacks clear documentation of accepted keys and values
body: The `--speculative-config` flag in vLLM’s CLI is referenced in the documentation, but the list of supported configuration keys, their expected data types, and permissible values is missing. Users are forced to guess the syntax (e.g., `draft_model=...`, `max_draft_len=...`, `num_speculative_tokens=...`) and often encounter parsing errors or silent failures on local hardware. This undocumented ambiguity hampers adoption of speculative decoding and leads to wasted troubleshooting time. **Relevant documentation:** - <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/spec_decode/#speculating-with-a-draft-model> - <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/#-speculative-config> 1. Add a dedicated “Speculative Config” section to the spec‑decode docs that enumerates all supported keys (e.g., `draft_model`, `max_draft_len`, `num_speculative_tokens`, `temperature`, `top_p`, etc.), their data types, default values, and allowed ranges. 2. Update the argument parser in the codebase to emit a clear error message when an unknown key or invalid value is supplied, and include a `--speculative-config-help` flag that prints the supported schema. Implementing these changes will make the feature discoverable, reduce user friction, and ensure consistent behavior across environments.

title: Handle OOV Multimodal Tokens Generically
body: Currently we have flags that are set on a per model basis for out of vocabulary tokens that indicate whether or not the tokens should be squeezed out prior to getting the LLM embeddings. I think it would be a good idea to simplify this to be generic, so that: - We remove the `handle_oov_mm_token` flag - When we initialize the model, we directly check if any multimodal tokens are OOV (i.e., register an arch's mm token indices at init time and just check against the vocab size) - Log once if multimodal tokens are OOV - At inference time, if the model has OOV multimodal tokens, mask with zeros to avoid incorrect placeholder offsets where it's expected, e.g., for LoRA This will resolve https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/29166 and is a cleaner alternative to the fix that I opened [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/32135), since it will avoid the extra flag + let us remove the current `handle_oov_mm_token` flag, as well as not have to worry about setting it for specific models in the future. If the cost of masking with zeros vs squeezing the IDs out is significant, we can also discuss what can be done there, but IMO it's worth trying to keep the offsets consistent where possible to avoid complexity unless benchmarks prove otherwise, since the cost of the one embedding lookup will be low relative to the overall generation @DarkLight1337 @jeejeelee @NickLucche @ywang96 Any thoughts? I will open a PR to discuss this more concretely as well

title: Eagle3 with tensor parallelism
body: According to https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/spec_decode/#speculating-using-eagle-based-draft-models: > The EAGLE based draft models need to be run without tensor parallelism (i.e. draft_tensor_parallel_size is set to 1 in speculative_config), although it is possible to run the main model using tensor parallelism (see example above). But there's no explanation for why the draft tpsize could only be set to 1, so I checked the code and found: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/52bf0665168c539d2d061a664ad62b18a12e80bb/vllm/config/speculative.py#L441-L447 and https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/52bf0665168c539d2d061a664ad62b18a12e80bb/vllm/config/speculative.py#L563-L571 I did not find any explicit restriction that enforces the draft model to run without tensor parallelism. So I guess the `draft_tensor_parallel_size` should be set to **either** 1 **or** the same value as the target_model. And also I tried doing so, and found that the tensor parallelism seems worked correctly. Is it possible that this functionality has already been implemented, but the documentation has not been updated accordingly? Just change one line of documentation as mentioned above: > It's possible to run the EAGLE based draft models with tensor_parallel using tp_size=1 or target_model_tpsize (i.e. `draft_tensor_parallel_size` is set to either 1 or the same value as the target_model in speculative_config).
